results.title: Sample Size and Power: How They Impact Research Significance
results.content: # What is the impact of sample size and power on the significance of research findings? If you are conducting market research, you need to know how sample size and power affect the significance of your findings. In this article, you will learn what sample size and power are, how they are related, and how they impact the significance of research findings. Sample size and statistical power significantly impact the significance and reliability of research findings. Power analysis serves as a crucial tool in research design, helping to determine the appropriate sample size needed to detect expected effects reliably. Sample size affects the significance of your research findings by influencing the standard error and the confidence interval of your estimates. Higher sample size allows the researcher to increase the significance level of the findings, since the confidence of the result are likely to increase with a higher sample size. Sample size directly influences the statistical significance of research findings. Adequate sample size enhances the chance of finding statistically significant results if a genuine effect exists, impacting the credibility and strength of research conclusions. Power affects the significance of your research findings by influencing the type II error and the effect size of your research. Researchers must balance sample size and power. To determine the optimal sample size and power for your research, you need to consider several factors, such as the level of significance, the type of test, the expected effect size, and the available resources. Power analysis helps estimate the sample size needed to detect significant effects or differences, ensuring the study has sufficient statistical power for reliable results. The relationship between sample size, power, and significance underscores the importance of careful consideration when designing marketing research studies. Adequate sample sizes and power calculations should be determined before conducting research to ensure that the study can effectively detect meaningful effects or differences. In summary, to obtain reliable and meaningful results, researchers need to carefully plan their studies considering both sample size and statistical power. An adequately powered study with a properly sized sample is more likely to yield results that are both statistically significant and practically important.

An important but difficult task in the design of a clinical trial to compare time to failure between two treatment groups is determination of the number of patients required to achieve a specified power of the test. Because patients typically enter the trial serially and are followed until they fail or withdraw from the study or until the study is terminated, the power of the test depends on the accrual pattern, the noncompliance rate, and the withdrawal rate in addition to the actual survival distributions of the two groups. Incorporating interim analyses and the possibility of early stopping into the trial increases its complexity, and although normal approximations have been developed for computing the significance level of the test when the log-rank or other rank statistics are used, there are no reliable analytic approximations for evaluating the power of the test. This article presents methods, based on Monte Carlo simulations and recent advances in group sequential testing with time-to-event responses, to choose appropriate test statistics, compute power and sample size at specified alternatives, check the adequacy of commonly used normal approximations of the type I error probability, and assess the performance of different interim analysis strategies.
